R_H1.passageTitle: From Public Consultation to an NHS Prescribing Rule

passages.label: A
passages.text: In England, homeopathy has long been a controversial part of health care. A proponent may value the choice to try it for particular symptoms. Critics ask whether the medical evidence is adequate for an NHS prescription. In 2017 NHS England began a public consultation about the kinds of item it should fund. The process collected views about individual choices as well as the burden on shared budgets. That raised a question about which forms of evidence could justify public spending.

passages.label: B
passages.text: NHS England opened a public consultation before making a decision. Patients, doctors, organisations and other members of the public could read the proposals and send comments. And the consultation covered all eighteen items, which together had cost about £141 million a year. This total was not the cost of homeopathy alone. A professional body could make a written contribution, and an individual patient could describe an experience. The process gathered views, but a personal story did not become scientific proof simply because it was sincere.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The evidence review asked a different question from the consultation. And it examined whether homeopathy had shown reliable benefits for particular conditions. NHS England reported that a review by the Specialist Pharmacy Service found no clear or robust evidence to support its use. A proponent might point to a patient who felt better, but improvement can have several causes. Symptoms can change naturally, expectations can affect how a person feels, and another treatment may be working at the same time. Controlled research tries to separate these explanations.

passages.label: D
passages.text: In November 2017, the NHS England board agreed that homeopathy should not be routinely prescribed in primary care. The decision was part of a wider plan concerning low-value items. A separate plan for common medicines sold without a prescription could save £190 million. This was not the saving from homeopathy or the eighteen items. Keeping these totals apart prevents a misleading impression about the cost of one treatment. The board said resources should support care with better evidence and reduce an avoidable financial burden.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Current NHS England guidance keeps the same direction. It advises prescribers not to start homeopathic items for new patients and to support existing patients in stopping them. The guidance places homeopathy in a group with low effectiveness, weak evidence or safety concerns. It does not prevent a patient from discussing symptoms with a clinician. A chief aim is to keep decisions connected to evidence while allowing a respectful conversation. A clinician can explain why conventional care has a stronger evidence base and what other help is available.

passages.label: F
passages.text: An account in favour of a therapy may describe how a patient seemed to recover, but a researcher still needs clinical data to judge whether it helped. An event that can occur after treatment cannot by itself prove that one product caused it. A trial can compare outcomes, including when symptoms improve, and it can make sure both groups receive urgent help where needed. Policymakers need a balance between listening to consultation views and using evidence about which therapies actually treat the condition.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A homeopathic product may sit beside a conventional drug on a store shelf, yet the two packages do not necessarily provide the same kind of information. Homeopathy began in Germany more than two hundred years ago. Its proponents claimed that a substance causing certain symptoms could treat similar symptoms when used in greatly diluted amounts. That principle remains controversial. For a reader comparing labels, the relevant questions concern the substances named, the actual amount in the product and the kind of medical evidence available.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Products may be sold as sugar pellets, liquids, gels, creams or tablets. Their ingredients can come from plants, minerals, chemicals, or animal and human sources. Labels often give Latin or scientific names for these substances. And they also show a dilution, such as 6X or 30C. In some products, repeated dilution may leave no measurable molecule of the original material, and the number on a label describes how a product was prepared. It does not by itself provide adequate evidence that the product can prevent or cure an illness.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A personal report can begin a useful question, but it cannot show cause on its own. A person may improve because an illness changes naturally, because another remedy is working, or because expectations affect the experience. A controlled study compares outcomes under planned conditions, and researchers need a precise question about a particular product and condition, and they also need a comparison group and a method that limits bias. Health claims are complex because the same change can have more than one possible explanation.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The word diluted can sound harmless, yet safety still requires attention, and some products have contained measurable amounts of active ingredients. Incorrect dilution, contamination or poor manufacturing can increase risk, and an ingredient can also interact with another drug. Consumers should report an adverse reaction and tell a doctor or pharmacist about every product they use. This information is especially important for children, pregnant people, older adults and anyone receiving care for a serious condition.

passages.label: E
passages.text: In the United States, a homeopathic label is not an FDA approval mark, and the FDA says no product labelled as homeopathic has been approved by the agency for any use. These products are subject to legal requirements for drugs, but products sold without approval have not passed the FDA review for safety and effectiveness, and a bottle may stand beside an approved medicine sold without a prescription in a shop. Its position on a shelf does not prove that the same review has taken place. A precise-looking code can appear on the packaging of a conventional pharmaceutical or a homeopathic product. Regardless of its format, the code alone cannot establish what evidence supports a treatment.

passages.label: F
passages.text: Bring the label when asking a health professional about a product offered as a therapy. An urgent symptom requires a timely assessment, and a new problem can occur while someone is trying a product. As a precaution, discuss other medicines, such as an antibiotic that a clinician has prescribed for an infection. A researcher comparing products in a clinical trial collects data over time. A single story of someone who seemed to recover cannot prove that a product will treat similar symptoms in another person.

R_H3.passageTitle: Building Universal Health Coverage in Thailand

passages.label: A
passages.text: Before universal coverage, Thailand had several public insurance schemes, but many people still lacked reliable access to care. Civil servants and formal employees were covered through existing arrangements, and people outside formal employment were more likely to face bills directly. A serious illness could create a heavy financial burden for a household, and the challenge was to reach citizens whose place in the labour market did not connect them to one of the established schemes.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The Universal Coverage Scheme began in 2001 for citizens who were not protected by the civil-service or social-security schemes. It was financed mainly from general government revenue rather than a separate payment collected from every member, and this meant that entitlement did not depend on an individual insurance contribution. The National Health Security Office was created to manage the scheme. Thailand still had three main public schemes, so universal coverage required coordination rather than replacing every existing arrangement with one office.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The programme became widely known through the phrase thirty baht treats all diseases. At the beginning, members made a small payment for a visit or hospital admission, although the scheme later removed that co-payment. The public message helped people understand that care was available, but the benefit package still had defined rules and some exclusions. A slogan could open the door to the system, and it could not explain every condition, referral or form of treatment.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Primary care formed the entrance to the scheme. Contracted hospitals organised local units, often serving about ten thousand to fifteen thousand people, and a patient normally began with the registered local network and was referred when more specialised care was needed. This structure supported continuity and helped direct hospital resources. It also required adequate staff, facilities and information, and a local consultation was therefore part of a connected path, not simply an isolated visit with no link to later care. Taxes help fund a service for people whose work arrangements do not provide regular insurance.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Studies described an increase in access after the change and a reduction in the number of households facing very high medical costs. A safety net can make it easier to see a professional regardless of their employment status. Earlier visits can help health services address symptoms or act to reduce the chance of a preventable illness. Access still depends on adequate staffing and supplies, so underfunding can leave some services hard to reach. The evidence about the financial burden should be read alongside information about where people received treatment and how long they waited.

passages.label: F
passages.text: The scheme has to maintain a balance between broad access and the staff and supplies available for clinical care. People needing urgent surgery or time on a hospital ward have different needs from those receiving regular therapy or physiotherapy. A researcher can examine data about who received these services and who continued to wait. A long-term assessment may look at prevention as well as the availability of an antibiotic or another medicine to treat a particular illness. The services offered affect what coverage means in daily life.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why did earlier coverage leave a gap for some citizens?
options: Existing insurance applied only to people who never paid medical bills.
People in jobs outside the established schemes were more likely to pay bills directly.
Everyone outside formal employment already belonged to the same public scheme.
The schemes were designed solely around where a patient entered a hospital.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What did the way the new scheme was funded change about access?
options: People saw a doctor only if they paid a separate insurance contribution beforehand.
It ended the use of all public revenue for health care.
Access through the scheme did not depend on each individual making an insurance contribution.
It required civil servants to leave existing arrangements before anyone could register.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does retaining three main schemes imply about starting the new one?
options: Different public arrangements still had to be coordinated.
The new office took over every existing insurance scheme.
Existing public arrangements stopped completely at the start.
Each person's access to publicly supported care had to end before a new scheme could begin.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why should someone not use the slogan as a complete account of the scheme?
options: It shows no one ever made a payment when using the scheme.

It requires every clinic to offer identical referrals and care.
It tells people about access without setting out all the benefits, limits or steps.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which sequence describes the usual path for someone needing more advanced care?
options: Start in a specialised ward, then apply to enter the country scheme.
Begin with the registered local service and be referred if needed.
Ask for a referral only after receiving all care without a local visit.
Treat the first consultation as separate from any later treatment.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why could a clearly advertised entitlement still lead to a difficult experience for some patients?
options: Advertising access ensures that each patient is seen at the same time.
Having a benefit package makes local staffing or facilities unnecessary.
Whether people can get the promised care also depends on the capacity of the local services.
All financial support applies only if a person pays a separate regular contribution.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How could a researcher check whether reduced household bills were accompanied by timely access?
options: Compare household costs with records of where and how long people waited for different kinds of care.
Use only the number of public announcements about coverage.
Ask which one of the schemes has the oldest name.
Count how many people read a slogan and treat the result as a measure of waiting.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What additional evidence would support a longer view of the scheme's effect?
options: Whether all hospital services require the same treatment and length of stay

Only how much one patient paid at a single visit
Evidence about preventing illness as well as the availability of treatment

questions.prompt: What links the need to reach people outside established insurance with the local organisation of care?
options: Eligibility can expand only if a patient first works in a formal job.
Public funding can reach people without established insurance, while local services give them a first point of contact.
A payment at the hospital by itself gives every household reliable access in advance.
Adding a source of revenue makes the location and capacity of care unimportant.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion fits how the article measures a broad health promise?
options: Coverage can be judged only by the wording of the public message.

Check who is eligible under the scheme's rules, what it does to household costs and which services patients can actually receive.
One reduction in costs establishes that every patient has equal access to every type of care.
